questions.label: Q1
questions.text:
It is hoped that a newly developed pain reliever will more quickly produce perceptible reduction in pain
to patients after minor surgeries than a standard pain reliever. The standard pain reliever is known to
bring relief in an average of 3.5 minutes with standard deviation 2.1 minutes. To test whether the new
pain reliever works more quickly than the standard one, 50 patients with minor surgeries were given the
new pain reliever and their times to relief were recorded. The experiment yielded a sample mean of 3.1
minutes and a sample standard deviation of 1.5 minutes. Is there sufficient evidence to indicate, at a 5%
level of significance, that the newly developed pain reliever does deliver perceptible relief more quickly?
questions.modelAnswer:
The natural assumption is that the new drug is no better than the old one. So, the new drug must be proved to be better. Thus if $\mu$ denotes the average time until all patients who are given the new drug experience pain relief, the null hypothesis is $H_0 : \mu = 3.5$ and the alternative hypothesis is that $H_1 : \mu < 3.5$. This is tested with significance level $\alpha = 0.05$.

Since the symbol in $H_1$ is $"<"$ this is a one-sided test and there is a single threshold value, $z_{0.05}$, so that $P(Z < z_{0.05}) = 0.05$. From table A3 we find that $z_{0.05} = -1.645$. So, the critical region is $(-\infty, -1.645]$.

The sample is large, but the population standard deviation is unknown (the 2.1 minutes pertains to the old drug, not the new one). Thus we use the test statistic $Z := \frac{\bar{X}-\mu}{S/\sqrt{n}}$, which, by the CLT, approximately has the standard normal distribution. Inserting the data into the formula for the test statistic gives us a realization of $z = \frac{3.1-3.5}{1.5/\sqrt{50}} = -1.886$.

The test statistic falls in the critical region, so we reject $H_0$. In the context of the problem our conclusion is: The data provide sufficient evidence, at the 5% level of significance, to conclude that the average time until patients experience perceptible relief from pain using the new pain reliever is smaller than the average time for the standard pain reliever.

Remark: We could also have calculated the p-value (in this case it is approximately 0.0294, check this for yourself), which is lower than $\alpha$, so we reject $H_0$.

questions.label: Q2
questions.text:
In the past the average length of an outgoing telephone call from a business office has been 143
seconds. A manager wishes to check whether that average has decreased after the introduction of policy
changes. A sample of 100 telephone calls produced a mean of 133 seconds, with a standard deviation of
35 seconds. Perform the relevant test at the 1% level of significance.
questions.modelAnswer: Notice that the 143 is old population data and it does not come from a random sample. So we want to check if the new population mean is below 143 or not. This gives rise to the following hypotheses: $H_0 : \mu = 143$ vs. $H_1 : \mu < 143$. Level of significance: $\alpha = 0.01$. Test statistic: $Z := \frac{\bar{X}-\mu}{S/\sqrt{n}} \approx N(0, 1)$ (by CLT). Under $H_0 : Z = \frac{\bar{X}-143}{35/\sqrt{100}}$. Realization: $z = \frac{133-143}{35/\sqrt{100}} = -2.86$. The critical region is $(-\infty, -2.33]$ (table A3). Therefore, we reject the null hypothesis $H_0$ (P-value: 0.0021).

questions.label: Q3
questions.text:
The average household size in a certain region several years ago was 3.14 persons. A sociologist
wishes to test, at the 5% level of significance, whether it is different now. Perform the test using the
information collected by the sociologist: in a random sample of 75 households, the average size was 2.98
persons, with sample standard deviation of 0.82 person.
questions.modelAnswer: $H_0 : \mu = 3.14$ vs. $H_1 : \mu \neq 3.14$ with level of significance $\alpha = 0.05$. Test statistic: $Z = \frac{\bar{X}-\mu}{s/\sqrt{n}} \approx N(0, 1)$ (by CLT). Under $H_0 : Z = \frac{\bar{X}-3.14}{0.82/\sqrt{75}}$. Realization: $z = \frac{2.98-3.14}{0.82/\sqrt{75}} = -1.69$. Critical region: $(-\infty, -1.96] \cup [1.96, \infty)$, so fail to reject $H_0$ (P-value: $2 \cdot 0.0455 = 0.0910$).

questions.label: Q4
questions.text:
The recommended daily calorie intake for teenage girls is 2,200 calories/day. A nutritionist at a
state university believes the average daily caloric intake of girls in that state to be lower. Test that
hypothesis, at the 5% level of significance, against the null hypothesis that the population average is
2200 calories/day using the sample data of size 36, mean 2150, standard deviation 203.
questions.modelAnswer: $H_0 : \mu = 2200$ vs. $H_1 : \mu < 2200$ (one-sided) with level of significance $\alpha = 0.05$. Test statistic: $Z = \frac{\bar{X}-\mu}{s/\sqrt{n}} \approx N(0, 1)$ (by CLT). Under $H_0 : Z = \frac{\bar{X}-2200}{203/\sqrt{36}}$. Realization: $z = \frac{2150-2200}{203/\sqrt{36}} = -1.478$. Critical region: $(-\infty, -1.645]$, so we do not reject $H_0$ (P-value: 0.0694).

questions.label: Q5
questions.text:
Suppose that a delivery company claims that they deliver their packages in 2 days on average, and
you suspect it’s longer than that. To test this claim, you take a random sample of 10 packages and record
their delivery times. You find the sample mean is $\bar{x} = 2.3$ days, and the sample standard deviation is
0.35. Do you have sufficient data to show that the company delivers their packages in more than 2 days,
considering significance level 0.05? And what assumptions do you need?
questions.modelAnswer:
Because $n = 10$ is much less than 30, and we don’t know the population standard deviation, the test statistic must be a t-distribution. This means that we need to assume that the data come from a distribution that is close enough to the normal distribution, so that we can use the test statistic $T = \frac{\bar{X}-\mu}{S/\sqrt{n}} \sim t_{n-1}$ (recall that a t-distribution is only allowed if the original data is ’approximately normal’). This is in practice an assumption that holds quite often, as long as the distribution is not too extreme and the sample size $n$ is not too small; as discussed in the lecture). The hypotheses: $H_0 : \mu = 2$ and $H_1 : \mu > 2$. Under $H_0 : T = \frac{\bar{X}-2}{0.35/\sqrt{10}}$. Realization: $t = \frac{2.3-2}{0.35/\sqrt{10}} = 2.71$. Critical region: $[1.833, \infty)$, so we reject $H_0$.

We can also ballpark the p-value: To do that look into table A4 in the row corresponding to $v = 9$. The test statistic falls between 2 values in this row: 2.574 and 2.821, corresponding respectively to columns 0.015 and 0.01. Thus, we know that the p-value for the test statistic $T$ lies between 0.01 and 0.015. So, we do not know the exact p-value, but because both 0.01 and 0.015 are below $\alpha = 0.05$, we reject $H_0$. and we have sufficient evidence that the average delivery time is more than 2 days.

questions.label: Q6(a)
questions.sharedContext:
An old research has determined the mean age of a certain population to be 70.65 with a 95 %
confidence interval of (67.2, 74.1). A new sample yields $\bar{x} = 75.32$.
questions.text: a) What is your conclusion concerning the $H_0 : \mu = 70.65$ with $\alpha = 0.05$?
questions.modelAnswer: Reject $H_0$ since $\bar{x}$ is outside the confidence interval.

questions.label: Q6(b)
questions.sharedContext:
An old research has determined the mean age of a certain population to be 70.65 with a 95 %
confidence interval of (67.2, 74.1). A new sample yields $\bar{x} = 75.32$.
questions.text: b) Is this a one-sided or a two-sided test?
questions.modelAnswer: This is a two-sided test since $\alpha$ is split into two probabilities of 0.025 on either side of the confidence interval.

questions.label: Q7(a)
questions.sharedContext:
The hypothesis $H_0 : \mu = 15$ is tested against $H_1 : \mu \neq 15$ with $\alpha = 0.05$. A random sample has
following properties: $n = 20$, $\bar{x} = 17.5$, $s = 5.9$.
questions.text: a) What assumptions should be made and which distribution should be used? Why?
questions.modelAnswer: Our distribution must not be too extreme (’approximately normal’). We then use $T = \frac{\bar{X}-15}{5.9/\sqrt{20}} \sim t_{19}$ (t-distribution with $v = 19$ degrees of freedom) as $n$ is small.

questions.label: Q7(b)
questions.sharedContext:
The hypothesis $H_0 : \mu = 15$ is tested against $H_1 : \mu \neq 15$ with $\alpha = 0.05$. A random sample has
following properties: $n = 20$, $\bar{x} = 17.5$, $s = 5.9$.
questions.text: b) What is the range of the P-value that you can find with table A4?
questions.modelAnswer: $2P\left(T = \frac{\bar{X}-15}{5.9/\sqrt{20}} > \frac{17.5-15}{5.9/\sqrt{20}}\right) = 2P(T > 1.895)$, where $P(T > 1.895)$ is between 0.025 and 0.05. So our P-value is between 0.05 and 0.10.

questions.label: Q7(c)
questions.sharedContext:
The hypothesis $H_0 : \mu = 15$ is tested against $H_1 : \mu \neq 15$ with $\alpha = 0.05$. A random sample has
following properties: $n = 20$, $\bar{x} = 17.5$, $s = 5.9$.
questions.text: c) What is your conclusion regarding the null hypothesis?
questions.modelAnswer: $P$-value is bigger than $\alpha$, thus we do not reject $H_0$.

questions.label: Q8
questions.text:
The average brown trout’s I.Q. is 4. Suppose you don’t believe this claim. You catch 12 brown trout.
A fish psychologist determines the I.Q.s as f ollows: 5; 4; 7; 3; 6; 4; 5; 3; 6; 3; 8; 5 . Conduct a hypothesis
test of your belief with $\alpha = 0.05$.
questions.modelAnswer: $H_0 : \mu = 4$, $H_1 : \mu \neq 4$. As our sample isn’t large enough to use CLT ($n < 30$), we should use a two-sided t-test with $\bar{x} = \frac{5+4+7+3+6+4+5+3+6+3+8+5}{12} = \frac{59}{12}$, $s = \sqrt{\frac{1}{11}\sum (x_i - \bar{x})^2} = 1.621$. We have to assume that the underlying distribution is not too extreme. The test statistic is $T = \frac{\bar{X}-\mu}{S/\sqrt{12}} \sim t_{11}$. Under $H_0 : T = \frac{\bar{X}-4}{1.621/\sqrt{12}}$. The acceptance region corresponding to a two-tailed t-test with $\alpha = 0.05$ is $(-2.201, 2.201)$. Realization: $T = 1.96$. So we do not reject $H_0$.

questions.label: Q9
questions.text:
A child psychologist says that the average time that working mothers spend talking to their children
is 11 minutes per day. Suppose a random sample of 100 working mothers spend on average 11.5 minutes
per day talking to their children. The prior research suggests the population standard deviation is 2.3.
Do we have evidence that working mothers spend more than 11 minutes per day by talking to their
children? Use $\alpha = 0.05$.
questions.modelAnswer: $H_0 : \mu = 11$, $H_A : \mu > 11$. Our test statistic is $\frac{\bar{x}-11}{2.3/\sqrt{100}} = 2.17$, corresponding to the $P$-value of 0.015, which is less than 0.05, thus we reject $H_0$. We have enough evidence to claim that working mothers spend more than 11 minutes per day by talking to their children.

questions.label: Q10
questions.text:
Consider the previous exercise, but now with a small change: The random sample does not include
100 working mothers, but only 10 working mothers. Will your conclusion change?
questions.modelAnswer: We need to use $t$−test (as $n$ is small), with $t_9 = \frac{\bar{x}-11}{2.3/\sqrt{10}} = \frac{11.5-11}{2.3/\sqrt{10}} \approx 0.6875$, which in table A.4 (row $v = 9$) lies between values 0.543 and 0.883, which correspond to $p$−values of 0.3 and 0.2, respectively, which are both bigger than $\alpha = 0.05$. Therefore, we do not have a sufficient evidence to reject $H_0$.

questions.label: Q11
questions.text:
The Achenbach Child Behaviour Checklist is designed so that scores from normal children are Normal
with mean $\mu = 50$ and standard deviation $\sigma = 10$. We are given a sample of $n = 5$ children under stress
with an average score of $\bar{x} = 56.0$. Is there evidence that children under stress show an abnormal
behaviour? You may assume that $\sigma$ still is known to be equal to 10. Use level of significance 0.05.
questions.modelAnswer: $H_0 : \mu = 50$, $H_1 : \mu \neq 50$ (two-sided), $\alpha = 0.05$. Under the null hypothesis, the stress scores of five children measured $X_1, \ldots, X_5 \sim N(50, 10)$, thus $Z = \frac{\bar{X}-\mu}{\sigma/\sqrt{5}} \sim N(0, 1)$. Realization: $z = \frac{\bar{x}-\mu}{\sigma/\sqrt{5}} = \frac{56-50}{10/\sqrt{5}} \approx 1.34$, while two-sided test with level of significance 0.05 corresponds to an acceptance region $(-1.96, 1.96)$, as $P(Z > 1.96) = P(Z < -1.96) = 0.025$. Therefore, we do not reject $H_0$, i.e. there is not significant evidence of abnormal behavior.

questions.label: Q12
questions.text:
Solve the previous exercise, assuming that we do not know $\sigma$, but are given a sample of $n = 5$ children
under stress with an average score of $\bar{x} = 56.0$ and standard deviation $s = 8.5$.
questions.modelAnswer: We have again $H_0 : \mu = 50$, $H_1 : \mu \neq 50$ (two-sided), $\alpha = 0.05$, $\bar{x} = 56$, $s = 8.5$. Under the null hypothesis $T := \frac{\bar{X}-50}{S/\sqrt{5}}$ is distributed according to a t-distribution with 4 degrees of freedom. Realization: $T = \frac{56-50}{8.5/\sqrt{5}} \approx 1.578$ which corresponds in our table A.4 to a p-value between 0.05 and 0.1 for a one-sided t-test, and thus a p-value between 0.1 and 0.2 for the two-sided t-test. This is more than the significance level $\alpha$, thus we do not reject $H_0$. Alternatively: The acceptance region for the two-sided $t_4$-distribution and $\alpha = 0.05$ is $(-2.776, 2.776)$ (table A4). Our test statistic clearly lies in this region, so we do not reject $H_0$.
